title: Generalized Newtonian, Bingham and conformation model equations

items.title: Generalized Newtonian, Bingham and conformation model equations
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; readiness recorded separately.
items.statement:
Use SI units and an oriented Euclidean three-space with Cartesian coordinates. Here $C^r$ means that coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open reference body with $C^1$ boundary, and let $\mathcal U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A smooth motion is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times\mathcal U;\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t(a):=\chi(t,a)$ is an orientation-preserving $C^2$ diffeomorphism onto its image; when labels are initially the current positions, $\chi_0(a)=a$. Set $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$. For $x\in\chi_t(\mathcal U)$ its inverse label map is $A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x)$, and its Eulerian velocity is $u(t,x)=\partial_t\chi(t,A(t,x))$. Position and material-label coordinates have units $\mathrm m$, time has units $\mathrm s$, and velocity has units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The velocity gradient is $L=\nabla u$, the rate-of-strain tensor is $D=(L+L^{\mathsf T})/2$, the spin is $W=(L-L^{\mathsf T})/2$, and the dilatation is $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{tr}L$; all have units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The material derivative is $D_t=\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla$, acting componentwise on tensor fields, with units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ on dimensionless fields. Matrix contraction is $S:T=\operatorname{tr}(S^{\mathsf T}T)$, with Frobenius norm $|S|=(S:S)^{1/2}$. These definitions are the mathematical motion and kinematics used below.

Write $\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)=\{D\in M_3(\mathbb R):D^{\mathsf T}=D,\operatorname{tr}D=0\}$. The generalized Newtonian branch is incompressible, so $\theta=0$ and $D\in\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)$. Define the shear-rate scalar $\dot\gamma=(2D:D)^{1/2}$, with units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and let $\eta(\dot\gamma)$ be a finite nonnegative viscosity with units $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$. The deviatoric stress is $\tau=2\eta(\dot\gamma)D$, in $\mathrm{Pa}$; no pressure term is included.

Two named viscosity choices are the Carreau form

$$
\eta_C(\dot\gamma)=\eta_\infty+(\eta_0-\eta_\infty)\bigl(1+(\lambda\dot\gamma)^2\bigr)^{(n-1)/2},
$$

with $\eta_0\ge\eta_\infty\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $\lambda\ge0$ in $\mathrm{s}$, and dimensionless $n>0$, and the regularized power form

$$
\eta_R(\dot\gamma)=m(\varepsilon^2+\dot\gamma^2)^{(n-1)/2},
$$

with $m>0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s^n}$, $\varepsilon>0$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and dimensionless $n>0$. For comparison, the unregularized power form $\eta_U=m\dot\gamma^{\,n-1}$ is defined only for $\dot\gamma>0$; its stress is extended by $\tau=0$ at $D=0$. When $0<n<1$, this viscosity diverges as $\dot\gamma\downarrow0$, although the extended stress may remain continuous.

For the Bingham branch use the Frobenius norm just defined, $\mu_p\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, and yield parameter $\tau_y\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Its set-valued deviatoric stress graph on $\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)$ is

$$
\mathcal B(D)=\begin{cases}\{2\mu_pD+\tau_yD/|D|\},&D\ne0,\\\{S\in\mathrm{Sym}_0(3):|S|\le\tau_y\},&D=0.\end{cases}
$$

The value at rest is therefore a whole stress ball when $\tau_y>0$. The chosen Frobenius normalization fixes the numerical convention for $\tau_y$; a source using a differently normalized second invariant requires a corresponding parameter conversion.

For the conformation branch, $C(t)$ is a dimensionless symmetric positive-definite $3\times3$ tensor, $G>0$ is a modulus in $\mathrm{Pa}$, $\lambda>0$ is a relaxation time in $\mathrm{s}$, and $\eta_s\ge0$ is a solvent viscosity in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$. Along an incompressible trajectory, adopt

$$D_tC-LC-CL^{\mathsf T}=-(C-I)/\lambda,\qquad \tau_p=G(C-I),\qquad \tau_s=2\eta_sD,\qquad w(C)=\frac G2\bigl(\operatorname{tr}C-\log\det C-3\bigr).$$

Here $\tau_p,\tau_s$ are polymer and solvent stresses in $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $w$ is a stored-energy density in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. The determinant in this formula is positive for symmetric positive-definite $C$, by the finite-dimensional real spectral theorem and determinant multiplicativity. These are mathematical constitutive definitions and adopted model equations. They assert neither empirical validity for a particular material nor existence of a solution to a fluid partial differential equation.

references.title: J. N. Reddy, An Introduction to Continuum Mechanics, Second Edition, Chapter 6, §§6.5.15 and 6.6.1–6.6.2.3
MIT OpenCourseWare, Lecture Notes on Fluid Dynamics (1.63J/2.21J), §1.6.2
John W. Barrett and Sebastien Boyaval, Existence and Approximation of a (Regularized) Oldroyd-B Model, arXiv:0907.4066v2, §1.1
S. Boyaval, T. Lelièvre, and C. Mangoubi, Free-energy-dissipative schemes for the Oldroyd-B model, ESAIM: M2AN 43 (2009), §§2.1.1–2.1.2

items.title: Objective generalized-Newtonian dissipation
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; readiness recorded separately.
items.statement:
Let $u$ be the $C^1$ Eulerian velocity induced by a $C^2$ incompressible motion in Euclidean three-space, and set $L=\nabla u$, $D=(L+L^{\mathsf T})/2$, and $\dot\gamma=(2D:D)^{1/2}$. Here incompressibility means $\operatorname{div}u=\operatorname{tr}L=0$. For any finite continuous viscosity $\eta:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ and the stress law $\tau=2\eta(\dot\gamma)D$, one has $\tau:D\ge0$. Under a $C^2$ rigid change of observer $x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, where $Q(t)\in SO(3)$, the transformed rate of strain is $D^*=QDQ^{\mathsf T}$, so the transformed stress is $\tau^*=Q\tau Q^{\mathsf T}$.

For the Carreau formula $\eta_C=\eta_\infty+(\eta_0-\eta_\infty)(1+(\lambda\dot\gamma)^2)^{(n-1)/2}$, assume $\eta_0\ge\eta_\infty\ge0$, $\lambda\ge0$, and $n>0$. It is finite and nonnegative for every finite $\dot\gamma$. If $\lambda>0$ and $\eta_0>\eta_\infty$, it decreases to $\eta_\infty$ for $0<n<1$, is the constant $\eta_0$ for $n=1$, and increases without bound for $n>1$; if $\lambda=0$ or $\eta_0=\eta_\infty$, it is constant. For the regularized power formula $\eta_R=m(\varepsilon^2+\dot\gamma^2)^{(n-1)/2}$, assume $m>0$, $\varepsilon>0$, and $n>0$; it is finite and strictly positive for every finite $\dot\gamma$. For the unregularized power stress $\tau=2m\dot\gamma^{n-1}D$ at $\dot\gamma>0$, with $m>0,n>0$, the extension $\tau=0$ at $D=0$ is continuous, even though the viscosity diverges there when $0<n<1$.

The dimensions are $[D]=[\dot\gamma]=[\varepsilon]=\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $[\eta]=[\eta_0]=[\eta_\infty]=[\eta_R]=[\eta_U]=\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $[\lambda]=\mathrm{s}$, $[m]=\mathrm{Pa\,s^n}$, and $[\tau]=\mathrm{Pa}$; $n$ is dimensionless.

references.title: J. N. Reddy, An Introduction to Continuum Mechanics, Second Edition, Chapter 6, §§6.5.15 and 6.6.1–6.6.2.3
MIT OpenCourseWare, Lecture Notes on Fluid Dynamics (1.63J/2.21J), §1.6.2

items.title: Bingham yield graph and convex monotonicity
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; readiness recorded separately.
items.statement:
Let $\mathcal S_0=\{D\in M_3(\mathbb R):D^{\mathsf T}=D,\operatorname{tr}D=0\}$, with Frobenius product $D:E=\operatorname{tr}(D^{\mathsf T}E)$ and norm $|D|=(D:D)^{1/2}$. For $D$ measured in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, let $\mu_p\ge0$ be in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$ and $\tau_y\ge0$ be in $\mathrm{Pa}$; define $\Phi(D)=\mu_p|D|^2+\tau_y|D|$, in $\mathrm{Pa\,s^{-1}}$, and

$$
\partial\Phi(D):=\{\tau\in\mathcal S_0:\Phi(E)\ge\Phi(D)+\tau:(E-D)\text{ for every }E\in\mathcal S_0\}.
$$

Define the Bingham graph by $\mathcal B(D)=\{2\mu_pD+\tau_yD/|D|\}$ when $D\ne0$, and by $\mathcal B(0)=\{\tau\in\mathcal S_0:|\tau|\le\tau_y\}$ when $D=0$; its graph stresses are in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Then $\Phi$ is finite, nonnegative, and convex; $\mathcal B(D)=\partial\Phi(D)$ for every $D$; the graph is monotone in the sense that $(\tau_1-\tau_2):(D_1-D_2)\ge0$ whenever $\tau_i\in\mathcal B(D_i)$; every graph value satisfies $\tau:D\ge0$; and, for $Q\in SO(3)$, $\mathcal B(QDQ^{\mathsf T})=Q\mathcal B(D)Q^{\mathsf T}$.

references.title: J. N. Reddy, An Introduction to Continuum Mechanics, Second Edition, Chapter 6, §6.6.2.3
MIT OpenCourseWare, Lecture Notes on Fluid Dynamics (1.63J/2.21J), §1.6.2

items.title: Objective conformation positivity and stored-energy dissipation
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; readiness recorded separately.
items.statement:
Let $T>0$, let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $[0,T]$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $u\in C^1(J\times\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ satisfy $\operatorname{div}u=0$ on a neighborhood of a $C^1$ trajectory $x:[0,T]\to\Omega$ with $x'(t)=u(t,x(t))$. Here $C^r$ means that coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous. Set $L(t)=\nabla u(t,x(t))$ and $D(t)=(L(t)+L(t)^{\mathsf T})/2$, both with units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Let $\mathrm{Sym}(3)$ denote the real symmetric $3\times3$ matrices and $\mathrm{Sym}^+(3)=\{M\in\mathrm{Sym}(3):v^{\mathsf T}Mv>0\text{ for every }v\ne0\}$. Let $C\in C^1([0,T];\mathrm{Sym}(3))$ be dimensionless and satisfy

$$
C'=LC+CL^{\mathsf T}-(C-I)/\lambda,\qquad C(0)=C_0\in\mathrm{Sym}^+(3),
$$

where $C_0\in\mathrm{Sym}^+(3)$, $G>0$ is in $\mathrm{Pa}$, $\lambda>0$ is in $\mathrm{s}$, and $\eta_s\ge0$ is in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$. Derivatives of $C$ at the endpoints are one-sided. Define $\tau_p=G(C-I)$ and $\tau_s=2\eta_sD$, both in $\mathrm{Pa}$. On $\mathrm{Sym}^+(3)$ define the stored-energy density $w(C)=\frac G2(\operatorname{tr}C-\log\det C-3)$ in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, where $\log r:=\int_1^r ds/s$ for $r>0$. Then $C(t)$ remains positive definite for every $t\in[0,T]$, $w(C(t))\ge0$, with equality exactly when $C(t)=I$, and for every $t$,

$$(\tau_s+\tau_p):D-\frac{d}{dt}w(C)=2\eta_sD:D+\frac{G}{2\lambda}\bigl(\operatorname{tr}C+\operatorname{tr}C^{-1}-6\bigr)\ge0.$$

For a $C^2$ rigid observer change $x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$ with $Q(t)\in SO(3)$, set $C^*=QCQ^{\mathsf T}$ and $L^*=QLQ^{\mathsf T}+Q'Q^{\mathsf T}$. The conformation equation is covariant under this transformation, $D^*=QDQ^{\mathsf T}$, $\tau_p^*=Q\tau_pQ^{\mathsf T}$, $\tau_s^*=Q\tau_sQ^{\mathsf T}$, and $w(C^*)=w(C)$. Positivity is a forward-time conclusion from the initial time $0$; no backward-time positivity, PDE solution existence, or entropy-production claim is asserted.

references.title: John W. Barrett and Sebastien Boyaval, Existence and Approximation of a (Regularized) Oldroyd-B Model, arXiv:0907.4066v2, §1.1
S. Boyaval, T. Lelièvre, and C. Mangoubi, Free-energy-dissipative schemes for the Oldroyd-B model, ESAIM: M2AN 43 (2009), §§2.1.1–2.1.2 and Appendix B, Lemma 2.1

title: Generalized Newtonian, Bingham and conformation model equations — Examples

items.title: The Bingham graph at zero contains nonzero tensors
items.design_state: Step 1 complete draft; readiness recorded separately.
items.statement:
Let $\tau_y>0$, let $D=0\in\mathrm{Sym}_0(3)$, and use the Frobenius-norm Bingham graph whose zero-rate value is $\{\tau\in\mathrm{Sym}_0(3):|\tau|\le\tau_y\}$. The tensor

$$
S=\frac{\tau_y}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&-1&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}
$$

is nonzero, trace-free, and has Frobenius norm $\tau_y$, so $S\in\mathcal B(0)$. Thus zero strain rate does not imply zero deviatoric stress in this set-valued Bingham model.

references.title: MIT OpenCourseWare, Lecture Notes on Fluid Dynamics (1.63J/2.21J), §1.6.2
